famous.historyContent:
The volcanic region around Kula was called Katakekaumene in ancient times. This expression means ''Burnt, Scorched Land''. This name is seen in the works of ancient writers such as Strabo of Amasya (54 B.C.–A.D. 24), Vitruvius (1st century B.C.), Stephanos of Byzantion (6th–7th century A.D.), and Eustathios (12th century A.D.).

Among these writers, Strabo is the one who describes Katakekaumene in the most detail. In his work, Strabo says:

“Then comes the land called Katakekaumene, which is 500 stadia (about 90 kilometers) long and 400 stadia (about 70 kilometers) wide. It is called both Mysia and Maionia. The Katakekaumene wine is not inferior to its rivals in quality. But outside the vineyards, everywhere is barren. The surface of the plain is covered with ash. The blackness of the mountainous and rocky land is attributed to the fires here. But some say this is the result of underground explosions and tell the legend of Typhon.
In fact, the reason the region became this way is the fire coming from underground. The sources from which this fire emerged are now gone. Here, there are three pits, 40 stadia apart from each other. The people call them 'bellows'. A hill rises next to each of them. It is thought that these hills were formed from the hot materials erupted from underground.”

In the section where he describes Phrygia, Strabo mentions Katakekaumene and also talks about the frequent earthquakes in the neighboring city of Philadelphia (Alaşehir):

“The reason for the name Katakekaumene is the constant shaking of the region. Even the city walls in Philadelphia are not safe because there are tremors and cracks every day. The people are used to these earthquakes and build their houses accordingly. Magnesia, at the foot of Mount Sipylos, suffered great damage from the great earthquake that occurred in our time, which destroyed Sardeis and many other famous cities. The emperor gave money to rebuild these cities.”

During the reign of the Roman Emperor Decius (A.D. 249–251), the leader Pionius, who was killed by pagans, interpreted the burnt appearance of the region as a punishment from God to the unbelievers:

“Do you not see the scorched land of Lydia, which is an example for the infidels?”

The A.D. 17 earthquake, also mentioned by Strabo, undoubtedly destroyed the Katakekaumene region. This great earthquake affected all of Western Anatolia and the Aegean islands. However, there is no information about the damage to the settlements around Kula.

It has been proven that Katakekaumene was the area between present-day Kula and Esenyazı in the south, the Gediz River in the north, Gökçeören (Menye/Maionia) in the west, and İncesu (Kollyda/Gölde) in the east. The cities of Maionia and Kollyda in this region were located on the King's Road, which started from Sardeis and went to the city of Susa of the Persians.

Other cities in the region are Thermai Theseos (Şehitlioğlu), Tabala (Güvercinlik), and Satala (Sandal). In addition, many ancient villages were found near the Gediz River: Koresa in Körez, Dora in Ayvatlar, Alkileura, Dima, Kerbia, and Axiotta around Hamidiye, and Iaza in Ayazören.

Between the 7th and 11th centuries, Kula was within the Opsikion Thema, one of the military and administrative regions of Byzantium. In Byzantium, the country was divided into regions called “Thema”. Each Thema was ruled by a commander. Opsikion was divided in two in the 9th century.

The Byzantine historian Pachymeres writes that Kula was a fortress that frequently changed hands between the Turks and the Byzantines. It is thought that the name Kula is related to the Turkish word “kale” (fortress). After it fell to the Turks, the Byzantines continued to use this name.

In 1306, Roger de Flor marched to Alaşehir with the Catalans under his command and captured Kula.

The Turkish period history of Kula becomes clear with the Germiyanid Principality. Mehmet Bey (1340–1361), son of the Germiyanid Bey Yakup Bey I (1300–1340), recaptured Kula and Simav, which the Catalans had taken from the Turks. This is stated in the stone foundation of Yakup Bey II as follows:

“My ancestor Mehmet Bey took Küldi (Kula) from the infidel. My ancestor Mehmet Bey also took Simav lake from the infidel. I have made it lawful for the remaining heirs and have endowed these.”

After Mehmet Bey, his son Süleyman Şah (1361–1387) succeeded him. Süleyman Şah wanted to get closer to the Ottomans due to political pressures and married his daughter Devlet Hatun to Yıldırım Bayezid, the son of Sultan Murad I. As a dowry, Kütahya, Tavşanlı, Simav, and Emet were given to the Ottomans, and Süleyman Şah made Kula the capital of the principality.

During the reign of Yıldırım Bayezid, Yakup Çelebi, the son of Süleyman Şah, tried to take back the lands given to the Ottomans, and the Germiyanid Principality was incorporated into the Ottoman lands.
After the Battle of Ankara in 1402, Timur gave these lands back to Yakup Bey. Yakup Bey came to Edirne in 1428, bequeathed his principality to Sultan Murad II, and passed away in 1429.

In the Ottoman period, Kula was administered as a district (kaza) subordinate to the Kütahya Sanjak. In 1852, upon the recommendation of the Governor of İzmir, the Kula district was attached to the Saruhan Sanjak.

After World War I, the Ottoman lands were occupied with the Armistice of Mudros (October 30, 1918). On May 15, 1919, the Greeks landed troops in İzmir with the support of the Allied Powers. They occupied Kula on June 28, 1920.
However, after the victory in the Great Offensive on August 30, 1922, the Greek forces retreated. On September 4, 1922, cavalry units under the command of Corps Commander Fahrettin Altay entered Kula and liberated the city.

Today, Kula is a city that still preserves all the traces of its history. It is a gateway opening from the past to the present.
